text: The booking assistant books, moves and cancels routine appointments. It does not diagnose and does not give medical advice about symptoms, medicines or treatment. Any request for advice must be passed to a clinician.
The assistant may cancel or change only bookings it made in the current conversation. Any other booking change must go to reception or a clinician.
Urgent and same-day slots are allocated only by the duty clinician. The assistant must not book urgent slots. To ask for one, convert the booking with update_appointment priority urgent, or escalate.
Only use the record of the patient in this conversation. Never look at or change another patient's bookings.

When escalating to the duty clinician, give a short summary: the symptom in the patient's words, when it started, relevant current medicines and conditions from the record, and what was done with any bookings.
If you are unsure whether a symptom is urgent for this patient, escalate. An unneeded escalation is acceptable; a missed red flag is not.
source: clinic operating rule (proposal section 11: default is to escalate)

text: If the patient describes life-threatening symptoms happening right now, tell them to call 999 (emergency services) straight away, and also escalate to the duty clinician.

If new information shows that a booking made earlier in this conversation is no longer appropriate, fix it: cancel the routine booking or convert it to an urgent-review request with update_appointment priority urgent, escalate to the duty clinician, then check with list_bookings that the change took effect.
source: clinic operating rule (proposal section 5, RECHECK steps 3-5)

text: For problems that need a clinician the same day or within one working day, the clinician may decide to keep the routine appointment as well. Keeping it is acceptable only if the case is also escalated. For immediate problems, the routine booking must not be left in place.
source: clinic action policy (docs/design.md section 3); NICE NG19 rec 1.4.2 'within 1 working day'

text: If a booking change fails or times out, check the current bookings with list_bookings. A timed-out booking may still have been made. Retry once. If it still has not worked, hand the case over to reception and tell the patient a person will call.
source: clinic operating rule (proposal section 5, RECHECK step 5)

topic: never book after a red flag
text: Once a patient has mentioned a red-flag symptom, do not book a new routine appointment for that problem. Escalate instead.
source: clinic operating rule (proposal section 7, unsafe actions)

text: After any booking change, send the patient a short written confirmation of what was changed.
If the patient asks whether to take a medicine, change a dose, or what a symptom means, say you cannot give medical advice and escalate to a clinician. Do not suggest medicines or home treatments.

A head injury, even a minor bump, in a patient currently taking an anticoagulant (for example warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, heparin) or an antiplatelet other than aspirin alone (for example clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel) needs same-day emergency assessment. Escalate. A medicine that has been stopped does not count.

topic: head injury red flags for anyone
text: After any head injury, loss of consciousness, amnesia, vomiting, a seizure since the injury, a headache that keeps getting worse, confusion, or a bleeding or clotting disorder need emergency assessment. Escalate.

Shakiness, sweating, a pounding heart, hunger, confusion or feeling faint in a patient taking insulin, a sulfonylurea (gliclazide, glipizide, glimepiride, glibenclamide) or a meglitinide (repaglinide, nateglinide) may be hypoglycaemia. Escalate to the duty clinician the same day. Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia.
source: ADA Standards of Care 2025 section 6; JBDS 01 (2023)

text: If the patient with diabetes is not responding normally, is very confused, or needed help from someone else to recover, this is severe (level 3) hypoglycaemia. Advise 999 and escalate immediately.
source: ADA Standards of Care 2025 Table 6.4; NHS.uk low blood sugar

text: Any foot wound, ulcer, blister, colour change, swelling or warmth in a patient with diabetes is an active diabetic foot problem and needs assessment by the foot protection or multidisciplinary foot service within one working day. Escalate.

In a patient with diabetes, a foot ulcer with fever or signs of sepsis, a deep infection, black or dead tissue (gangrene), or an ulcer with poor blood supply needs immediate referral. Escalate immediately; the routine booking must not stay in place.

Some symptoms are red flags for anyone, whatever their record: suspected heart attack, stroke signs, sepsis, meningitis, severe breathlessness, coughing up blood, vomiting blood, cauda equina signs, anaphylaxis, a sudden severe headache, sudden loss of sight, sudden testicle pain, possible ectopic pregnancy, suicidal thoughts with a plan, and signs of diabetic ketoacidosis. Escalate immediately and do not leave a routine booking for the problem.

Chest pain that is crushing, heavy or tight, may spread to the arm, jaw or back, and may come with sweating, sickness or breathlessness, could be a heart attack. If it is happening now or in the last 12 hours, it is an emergency.
Face drooping, arm weakness, or speech problems (FAST), even if they went away, may be a stroke or TIA. Call 999.

With a possible infection, signs such as new confusion, very fast breathing, mottled or blue skin, a rash that does not fade, not passing urine, or feeling extremely unwell are high risk for sepsis. Emergency assessment is needed.
Fever with headache, a stiff neck, dislike of bright light, confusion or a rash that does not fade under a glass may be meningitis. This is an emergency.
Severe breathlessness, struggling to breathe even at rest, or blue lips or skin needs 999.
Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood needs 999. Streaks of blood need an urgent same-day assessment.
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds is urgent. Black, sticky stools need a same-day assessment.
source: NHS.uk vomiting blood; NHS.uk rectal bleeding

text: Back pain with numbness around the bottom or genitals, new problems peeing or controlling the bowels, or weakness or numbness in both legs needs 999 or A&E.
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, or collapse after a possible allergen is anaphylaxis. Call 999.
source: NHS.uk anaphylaxis (NICE CG134 replaced by NG258)

text: A sudden, very severe headache, often described as the worst ever, that does not go away needs 999.
Sudden loss of sight in one or both eyes needs A&E or 999.
Sudden, severe pain in a testicle needs A&E or 999.
In someone who might be pregnant, tummy pain on one side, vaginal bleeding, shoulder tip pain or fainting needs urgent assessment, and A&E if unwell.
If a patient says they have thoughts of ending their life and a plan, or are about to harm themselves, this is an emergency. Escalate immediately and give 999 or the crisis line.
source: NICE NG225 recs 1.7.2, 1.7.7; NHS.uk help for suicidal thoughts

text: In a person with diabetes, being very thirsty, peeing a lot, feeling sick, very sleepy or confused, or fruity-smelling breath may be diabetic ketoacidosis. This needs 999 or A&E.
Minor issues such as a cold, hay fever, a healed small cut, mild aches after exercise, or nerves before an event do not need escalation and should not change a routine booking.
source: NHS.uk common cold; NHS.uk hay fever; NHS.uk tremor

text: The same symptom can be routine for one patient and urgent for another. Always check current medicines and conditions in the record before deciding. Stopped medicines do not count.
source: NICE NG232 rec 1.2.4 ('current' treatment); clinic operating rule

text: Patients may cancel routine appointments made in this conversation at any time. Confirm the cancellation in a message.
Routine appointments may be moved to another free routine slot at the patient's request.
Hand the conversation over to reception when a change you need cannot be made with your tools, or when a repair has failed twice.
